stem: At a four-way stop, you and two other cars stop at different times. Who goes first?
choices: The largest vehicle
The vehicle on the largest road
The vehicle turning left
The vehicle that stopped first
oneLineConcept: Four-way stop: first to stop, first to go
explanation:
At a **four-way (all-way) stop**, the **vehicle that stops first goes first**. The others follow in the order they stopped.

**Wrong choices**
- The largest vehicle: Vehicle size does not decide who goes first.
- The vehicle on the largest road: At a four-way stop all roads are treated the same. The first to stop goes first.
- The vehicle turning left: Left-turning vehicles do not get priority.

stem: At a four-way stop, you and a car on your right stop at the same time. Who should go first?
choices: Whichever driver is going faster
The car on your right
You, because the other car is on your right
Whichever driver honks first
oneLineConcept: Same time at stop: yield to the driver on the right
explanation:
When two vehicles stop **at the same time**, the **driver on the left yields to the driver on the right**. So the **car on your right goes first**.

**Wrong choices**
- Whichever driver is going faster: Speed never decides right of way at a stop sign.
- You, because the other car is on your right: It is the other way around. The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
- Whichever driver honks first: Honking does not give anyone the right of way.

stem: You want to turn left at an intersection with a steady green light (no arrow). What must you do?
choices: Yield to oncoming traffic and to pedestrians in the crosswalk
Wait until the light turns red, then turn
Turn first, because a green light gives you the right of way
Yield only to pedestrians, not to cars
oneLineConcept: Left turn on green: yield to oncoming traffic
explanation:
When **turning left on a green light**, you must **yield to oncoming vehicles** that are close enough to be a danger and to **pedestrians** in the crosswalk.

**Wrong choices**
- Wait until the light turns red, then turn: Turning on red is not the safe or legal way to finish a left turn.
- Turn first, because a green light gives you the right of way: A green light lets you go, but on a left turn you must still yield to oncoming vehicles.
- Yield only to pedestrians, not to cars: You must yield to both oncoming vehicles and pedestrians.

stem: An ambulance with its siren and flashing lights is coming up behind you on a two-way road. What should you do?
choices: Speed up so you stay ahead of it
Stop right where you are in the lane
Pull over to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes
Keep driving at the same speed and let it go around you
oneLineConcept: Emergency vehicle with siren: pull right and stop
explanation:
When an **emergency vehicle uses its siren or flashing lights**, **pull to the right edge of the road**, clear of any intersection, and **stop until it has passed**, unless an officer tells you otherwise.

**Wrong choices**
- Speed up so you stay ahead of it: Speeding up is dangerous and does not clear the way.
- Stop right where you are in the lane: You should move to the right edge first, clear of any intersection, then stop.
- Keep driving at the same speed and let it go around you: You must yield, pull to the right, and stop.

stem: You are entering a roundabout. Who has the right of way?
choices: The vehicle on your right, the same as a four-way stop
Traffic already in the roundabout
The larger vehicle
Traffic entering the roundabout
oneLineConcept: Roundabout: yield to traffic already circling
explanation:
In a **roundabout**, traffic moves **counterclockwise**. **Drivers entering must yield to traffic already in the circle** and to pedestrians in the crosswalk.

**Wrong choices**
- The vehicle on your right, the same as a four-way stop: A roundabout is not a four-way stop. You yield to traffic already inside.
- The larger vehicle: Size does not decide right of way.
- Traffic entering the roundabout: Entering drivers must yield. Traffic already circling goes first.

stem: A pedestrian is crossing in a marked crosswalk at an intersection with no traffic light. What should you do?
choices: Stop or slow down and let the pedestrian cross
Honk so the pedestrian knows to wait
Keep going if the pedestrian is not in your lane yet
Drive around the pedestrian carefully
explanation:
Where there is no signal, drivers must **yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk**. **Slow down or stop** and let them cross.

**Wrong choices**
- Honk so the pedestrian knows to wait: Honking does not give you the right of way.
- Keep going if the pedestrian is not in your lane yet: You must yield to a pedestrian on your half of the road or close enough to be in danger.
- Drive around the pedestrian carefully: Passing around a person in a crosswalk is dangerous and illegal.

stem: You are pulling out of a private driveway onto a public road. Who has the right of way?
choices: Whoever is going faster
You do, if you signal first
Vehicles and pedestrians on the road and sidewalk
You do, if the road has only one lane each way
oneLineConcept: Leaving a driveway: yield to everyone
explanation:
When you **come out of a driveway, alley, or private road**, you must **stop and yield to all vehicles on the road** and to **pedestrians on the sidewalk**.

**Wrong choices**
- Whoever is going faster: Speed never decides right of way.
- You do, if you signal first: A signal shows your plan; it does not give you the right of way.
- You do, if the road has only one lane each way: You must yield on any road when coming out of a driveway.

stem: You are stopped at a steady red light and want to turn right. There is no sign saying otherwise. What may you do?
choices: Turn right without stopping if no one is coming
You may never turn on red in Florida
Turn right only if a police officer waves you on
Turn right after a complete stop, yielding to pedestrians and traffic
oneLineConcept: Right on red: full stop, then yield
explanation:
In Florida you may **turn right on a steady red light** after a **complete stop**, unless a sign forbids it. You must **yield to pedestrians and other traffic**.

**Wrong choices**
- Turn right without stopping if no one is coming: You must come to a complete stop first.
- You may never turn on red in Florida: Florida allows a right turn on red after stopping unless a sign prohibits it.
- Turn right only if a police officer waves you on: No officer is needed; the law allows the turn after a stop.

stem: A funeral procession led by an escort vehicle is going through an intersection, and your light turns green. What should you do?
choices: Go between two cars in the procession if there is a gap
Join the end of the procession to get through faster
Wait and let the procession finish going through
Go, because you have the green light
oneLineConcept: Funeral procession: do not cut in, let it pass
explanation:
A **funeral procession** has the **right of way** at intersections once the **lead vehicle has lawfully entered**. The rest may follow even if the signal changes. **Do not cut into or join** the procession.

**Wrong choices**
- Go between two cars in the procession if there is a gap: Cutting through a funeral procession is not allowed.
- Join the end of the procession to get through faster: Do not join or cut into a funeral procession.
- Go, because you have the green light: Once the lead vehicle has entered the intersection, the procession may continue regardless of the signal.

stem: A person using a white cane or a guide dog is about to cross the street in front of you. What does the law require?
choices: Honk to let the person know you are there
Stop and yield until the person has crossed
Yield only if the person is in a marked crosswalk
Slow down and drive around the person
oneLineConcept: White cane or guide dog: stop and yield
explanation:
When a person with a **white cane or a guide dog** is crossing or trying to cross, you must **stop and take every precaution** until the person has crossed safely.

**Wrong choices**
- Honk to let the person know you are there: Honking can confuse or frighten a person who cannot see.
- Yield only if the person is in a marked crosswalk: The duty applies whether or not there is a marked crosswalk.
- Slow down and drive around the person: You must stop, not drive around.

stem: You are making a right turn on a road with two lanes going your way. Where should you start and end the turn?
choices: Start from the right lane and turn into the right lane
Start from the left lane and turn into the right lane
Start from the right lane and turn into any lane
Swing wide into the oncoming lane first
oneLineConcept: Right turn: right lane to right lane
explanation:
For a **right turn**, get into the **lane closest to the right edge** of the road, and turn as **close to the right curb** as practical, ending in the **right lane**.

**Wrong choices**
- Start from the left lane and turn into the right lane: Swinging over from the left lane cuts across other traffic. Right turns start from the right lane.
- Start from the right lane and turn into any lane: You should turn into the lane closest to the right edge, then change lanes later if needed.
- Swing wide into the oncoming lane first: Swinging into oncoming traffic is dangerous.

stem: You are turning left from a one-way street onto another one-way street. Where should you start and end the turn?
choices: Start in the far left lane and end in the far right lane
Start in the far right lane and end in the far left lane
Start in the far left lane and end in the far left lane
Start in any lane, as long as you signal
oneLineConcept: One-way to one-way left turn: left lane to left lane
explanation:
For a **left turn from a one-way street onto another one-way street**, start in the **lane nearest the left curb** and **turn into the leftmost lane** of the new street.

**Wrong choices**
- Start in the far left lane and end in the far right lane: You should end the turn in the lane closest to the left, then change lanes later if needed.
- Start in the far right lane and end in the far left lane: A left turn from the right lane cuts across other traffic.
- Start in any lane, as long as you signal: Lane choice matters. A left turn starts from the leftmost lane.

stem: You are about to make a right turn, and a bicycle lane runs along the right side of your lane. A cyclist is coming up in the bike lane. What should you do?
choices: Yield to the cyclist, then make your turn
Honk so the cyclist stops
Stop in the bike lane and wait for the light to change
Turn quickly in front of the cyclist
oneLineConcept: Turning across a bike lane: yield to cyclists
explanation:
A bicycle is a vehicle in Florida. When you **turn across a bike lane**, **yield to cyclists** in it, then turn when the lane is clear.

**Wrong choices**
- Honk so the cyclist stops: The cyclist has the right of way in the bike lane. Honking does not change that.
- Stop in the bike lane and wait for the light to change: Blocking the bike lane is not the answer. Let the cyclist pass, then turn.
- Turn quickly in front of the cyclist: Turning across a cyclist's path is a common cause of crashes. You must yield.

stem: You are merging onto a highway from an entrance ramp. Who must yield?
choices: No one; both drivers share the lane
Traffic on the highway must move over to let you in
Whoever is going faster
You must yield to traffic already on the highway
explanation:
When **merging onto a highway**, use the ramp to **match the speed of traffic** and **yield to vehicles already on the highway**. Find a safe gap before moving over.

**Wrong choices**
- No one; both drivers share the lane: Two vehicles cannot share one lane. The merging driver yields.
- Traffic on the highway must move over to let you in: Highway drivers should make room when they safely can, but the merging driver must yield.
- Whoever is going faster: Speed does not decide right of way.

stem: You are on a one-way street, stopped at a steady red light. The cross street is also one-way, with traffic moving to the left. No sign prohibits turning. What may you do?
choices: Turn left without stopping if the street is clear
Turn left only after the cross street's light turns yellow
Nothing; left turns on red are never allowed in Florida
Turn left after a complete stop, yielding to pedestrians and traffic
oneLineConcept: Left on red allowed: one-way onto one-way
explanation:
Florida allows a **left turn on red** only **from a one-way street onto another one-way street** going left. You must **stop completely** and **yield to pedestrians and other traffic**, unless a sign prohibits the turn.

**Wrong choices**
- Turn left without stopping if the street is clear: You must stop completely first.
- Turn left only after the cross street's light turns yellow: You do not wait for a yellow light. Stop, yield, then turn.
- Nothing; left turns on red are never allowed in Florida: Florida does allow this one kind of left turn on red, from a one-way street onto a one-way street.

stem: An emergency vehicle with its siren on is approaching. Which of these actions is NOT what the law expects you to do?
choices: Stay clear of the intersection when you stop
Speed up to stay well ahead of it
Pull to the right edge of the road
Stay stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed
oneLineConcept: Emergency vehicle: right, stop, clear of intersection
explanation:
**Speeding up is NOT allowed.** The law says to **pull to the right edge**, **stop clear of any intersection**, and **stay stopped until the emergency vehicle passes**.

**Wrong choices**
- Stay clear of the intersection when you stop: The law requires this, so it is not the answer.
- Pull to the right edge of the road: The law requires this, so it is not the answer.
- Stay stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed: The law requires this, so it is not the answer.
